title: The Rat, the Clock, and the Little Wobbly Bit
markdown:
In the highest sun-drenched nook of Oakhaven, among lavender bushes and the whisper of morning dew, Professor Fitzwilliam Tick-Tock kept a workshop that smelled faintly of singed toast. Gears, springs, and tiny gleaming tools covered every surface in an order only he claimed to understand. His whiskers twitched with a thousand brilliant, sometimes half-baked ideas. Rosa the hedgehog sat in the doorway, stout-hearted, sensible-spined, the calm in his magnificent whirlwind. She found the tinkering fascinating even when it produced a puff of smoke or a scattering of errant springs.

The Great Town Clock usually laid a gold face over the square, a beacon of punctuality the town trusted the way it trusted bread. This morning its ornate hands were stuck at noon. No tick. A hush thick as Oakhaven fog gathered under it. Shop doors stayed half open. A pigeon on the minute-hand looked personally offended. The Mayor, a portly badger with a voice that could rumble like distant thunder, stood beneath the silent titan and asked who, with skill and daring, might mend it before schedules unravelled completely.

Fitzwilliam, who had of course been listening from his rooftop with a gleaming brass spyglass, felt the familiar insistent twitch in his tail that meant a grand gesture was loading. He scurried to the roof’s edge, tiny chest puffed with almost comical pride. “Fear not, worthy Mayor. Professor Fitzwilliam Tick-Tock, at your service. I shall have this mechanism singing before the sun dips west.”

Rosa nudged him with her snout. “Fitzwilliam, my dear friend, are you quite certain? The Great Clock is very great. And very old. Its workings are legend.”

He waved a dismissive paw. “Instructions are for those who lack spark. I shall eye its peculiarities and coax it back with genius.” He believed it hard enough to ignore the other fact, the one he seldom confessed when pride was piqued: last autumn he had flourished the ancient leather-bound manual and declared it mastered. He could not now remember which shelf, which lavender pot, which promising heap of springs held it.

They went down from the rooftop kingdom. Rosa carried a well-organized toolbox over her shoulder. The interior of the tower was a labyrinth of brass and iron, a forest of gears with phantom memories of hours. Dust motes turned in a shaft of light that no longer meant midday, because midday had got stuck. Fitzwilliam set to work with a dramatic flourish and a determined glint. He hummed a jaunty, off-key tune, a sure sign his mind was a hive.

He fiddled a cog here, a small spring there. A particularly large, vital wheel, meant to mesh with another, stubbornly refused. It was as if the wheel had inherited a silent streak from generations of time-keepers. He poked it. He prodded it with a tiny screwdriver. In a moment of desperate inspiration he offered it a crumb of aged cheddar, as if dairy might sway the heart of time. The wheel remained. A faint acrid puff rose from a nearby joint. Rosa did not comment. Her silence had opinions.

A small, clear voice piped from the shadowy doorway. “Excuse me, Mister Rat?”

Lily, the baker’s daughter, stood there with a wilting dandelion clock, its fluff poised to scatter. Her eyes held the bright, untainted wonder of unanswered questions. “Mum said you were fixing the Great Clock. It’s very important. Everyone is waiting. But what does that little, wobbly bit do?”

She pointed an earnest finger at a peculiar, almost decorative lever Fitzwilliam had been studiously ignoring. Too insignificant. Too trivial. An afterthought in a magnificent design.

He froze mid-fiddlement. Rosa peered too. Below, townsfolk had quietly assembled, faces a mixture of hope and the particular anxiety of people who did not know when lunch was. The little, wobbly bit. No one had ever really asked. It looked like show.

Fitzwilliam’s mind, usually a symphony of escapements and calculations, went silent. He knew every pendulum, every chime. The wobbly bit had never been a question he allowed. The forgotten manual flickered behind his eyes, last autumn’s flourish, the leather smell, the way he had closed it without needing the last chapter.

He saw Lily’s expectant face. The Mayor’s furrowed frown. Rosa’s patient gaze, a testament she would not hurry into a lie. For the first time that morning, not knowing felt like a measurement rather than a collapse.

He looked at the lever, then at the still wheel. He did not make a speech for the square. He reached out and, with a gentle, almost imperceptible nudge, set the little wobbly bit a hair to the left.

The great wheel gave a soft, satisfying clunk and began to turn, slow as a thought, then sure. Smaller gears found their partners. A magnificent tick-tock-tick-tock moved through the tower, down the streets, into the hearts of everyone gathered. The frozen hands remembered how to sweep. Noon, embarrassed, agreed to leave.

A cheer rose, a wave of sound. The Mayor let out a joyful booming bellow. Fitzwilliam’s fur was ruffled from exertion; he bowed because he was, still, a showman. He had not needed the manual in his paw. He had needed a question he did not fake an answer to.

Rosa smiled, rare and wide, snout crinkling. “Well done, Fitzwilliam. Magnificently done.”

Lily blew. Dandelion fluff lifted past the newly moving hands, pale against brass, and drifted out into a noon that was no longer stuck. A pigeon rearranged itself, mollified. Fitzwilliam left the wobbly bit where Lily’s finger had taught it to be. The clock, unconsulted by any shelf, kept on, and the lavender on the roof, when they climbed back, smelled of ordinary continuing time.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
